lesson.title: The -ation Engine
lesson.subtitle: Noun → verb: confirmation → confirmer. Thousands of infinitives, almost free

hook.title: The Verbs Were Hiding in the Nouns
hook.content: Every -ation noun carries its verb inside it. The confirmation? To confirm. The organisation? To organise. French does this mechanically: strip -ation, bolt on -er (pronounced /e/), and the noun becomes the infinitive: confirmation → confirmer, organisation → organiser. One rule, thousands of verbs — this is the single most valuable conversion in the language.

footnotes.title: The test
footnotes.content: Ask: is there an -ation word in English for this idea? Reservation → yes → réserver. That question is your verb-finder for life.

pattern.title: je veux + Infinitive — and the Célébrer Trap
pattern.content: French needs no 'to': the verb itself is the dictionary form. je veux confirmer — I want to confirm. je veux visiter Paris. One idea (to visit), one word (visiter). But watch the trap: célébration → célébrer, never célébrater. The whole -ation goes before -er arrives — strip, don't trim.

footnotes.title: Register travels in reverse
footnotes.content: 'I want to participate' sounds formal in English; je veux participer is perfectly everyday. Don't decide too quickly that you can't say something — look for the -ation word first.

pattern.linguist_note: French -er descends from Latin -āre. The -ation nouns and the -er verbs are two leaves of the same Latin branch — which is why the conversion loses almost nothing.
pattern.trap_note: The shortcut your mind will offer: jump straight from the English verb to a French one — celebrate → célébrater. Wrong. Convert the noun, then strip it whole: célébration → célébrer.

exercises.prompt: Strip -ation from 'confirmation' and attach the French infinitive ending:
exercises.explanation: confirm + er = confirmer (/kɔ̃fiʁme/). Strip the whole -ation suffix and add -er.

exercises.prompt: Apply the engine — carefully: célébration → French verb:
exercises.explanation: The trap in action: the whole -ation goes. célébration → célébrer, not célébrater.

exercises.idea: you want to celebrate — the exam results just came in
cues: je veux + infinitive: je veux célébrer
exercises.explanation: je veux célébrer — two words in French where English needs three.

diagnosis.cue: Strip, don't trim: célébration loses ALL of -ation before -er lands. célébrer, never célébrater.

exercises.prompt: Which English sentence is built the French way?
exercises.meaning: The odd English is the lesson: French joins want + visit directly with no 'to'.
exercises.explanation: Je veux visiter Paris is word-for-word 'I want visit Paris'. French chains the infinitive directly — no 'to' needed.

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the whole sentence.
exercises.meaning: Do you want to get involved?
cues: the -er sounds like /e/: participé? — no: participer with a tiny final r
exercises.explanation: participer — 'to get involved' sounds formal in English and everyday in French.
exercises.affirmation: You heard the /e/ ending and kept the final r light — that's the infinitive's sound.

summary.outcome: Convert any -ation noun into an -er verb, chain it after je veux, and dodge the célébrer trap.

use_example.english: I want to reserve a table.

summary.takeaway: Find the -ation noun, strip it whole, add -er — and let je veux pull it into a sentence.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next on Le Pont ([301] The Célébrer Trap): see how The -ation Engine leads directly into The Célébrer Trap.

payoff.text: The -ION warehouse from Lesson 2 was secretly a verb factory: stripping -ation and adding -er turns your noun shelf into active verbs.

foreshadow.line: You can say everything you want to do — next we wrap the verb in two small words to refuse it.

twist.prompt: Ungraded — how would you say 'I want to reserve the table'?
twist.explanation: réservation → réserver, chained directly after je veux with no extra word for 'to'.

confirmer.etymology_derivation: confirmation → confirmer. Strip -ation, bolt on -er (pronounced /e/), and the noun becomes the verb.

organiser.etymology_derivation: organisation → organiser. One S in French, even where English writes Z.

célébrer.etymology_derivation: célébration → célébrer. The trap: not *célébrater — the whole -ation goes before -er arrives.

participer.context_translation: I want to get involved a little.
participer.etymology_derivation: participation → participer. 'To get involved' sounds formal in English but everyday in French — register travels in reverse.

visiter.etymology_derivation: visitation → visiter. The rare English noun unlocks the everyday verb: don't decide too quickly that you can't say it.

inviter.context_translation: Do you want to invite Marie?

réserver.context_translation: I want to reserve a table.

vouloir.etymology_derivation: Latin volō 'I want' → vouloir. A volunteer is the one who wants to do — the want-root English kept in voluntary, benevolent.

ation.name: The -ation Engine
ation.historical_linguistics: French -er verbs descend from Latin -āre; the English -ation nouns and French verbs are two leaves of the same Latin branch, so the noun unlocks the verb with almost no loss.
ation.philological_note: The whole -ation goes — célébration → célébrer, never *célébrater. Test for the -ation noun in English first; it is the proof the verb converts.
ation.literature_source: Guillaume, Temps et verbe (1929); standard French morphophonology.
